method_note: Every government site (ontario.ca, canlii.org, all municipal sites) refused direct fetches from this sandbox. All findings come from web-search result summaries and snippets, not from reading the full by-law or regulation text. Segment endpoints in particular came from truncated snippets. Treat everything here as a lead to verify, and confirm the current text on e-Laws and each municipality's site before relying on it.

provincial.summary: Framework: HTA s.191.8 plus O. Reg. 316/03 (Operation of Off-Road Vehicles on Highways). s.2: no ORV on any highway except as the regulation permits, as Part IV permits, or as ORV Act cl. 2(2)(a) permits (direct crossing). s.3: no ORV on any highway in Schedule A ('highways prohibited to all off-road vehicles'). Schedule A covers the 400-series and QEW, plus named segments of King's highways (some found in the bbox are listed under highways). s.4: Schedule B highways are closed except to ATVs, two-up ATVs, ROVs, MOHUVs, ETVs and off-road motorcycles that meet Part III. MTO summary: permitted ORVs may use Highways 500-899, many 7000-series highways and some low-traffic highways, but not 400-series, the QEW or sections of the Trans-Canada. Part III conditions when on a highway: ride on the shoulder in the direction of traffic, as close to the right edge as practicable. Use the travelled lane only if the shoulder is unsafe, obstructed or too narrow to keep all tires off the roadway. Never ride in the median. Speed limits are 20 km/h where the posted limit is 50 km/h or less, and 50 km/h where it is over 50 km/h; a by-law may set a lower one. Driver must be 16+ with a G2/M2 or higher licence. Vehicle must have a permit, a rear plate and insurance, and the rider an approved helmet (seatbelts where fitted). Headlights and taillights stay on. A single-rider ATV may carry no passenger; on-road passengers on two-up machines must be 8+. Highways inside provincial parks are open only if the park permits ORVs (Algonquin does not). Municipal roads: an ORV may use a municipal highway only if a s.191.8(3) by-law permits it. Exception since Jan 1, 2021 (O. Reg. 740/20): in municipalities listed in O. Reg. 8/03 (former townships where the 80 km/h default applies), ORVs that meet 316/03 are allowed on municipal roads by default unless a by-law prohibits or restricts them. Elsewhere (towns, cities), no by-law means no on-road riding. Municipal by-laws may also limit months, hours, vehicle types, speeds and specific roads. Unverified: whether King's highways that are in neither Schedule A nor B are open by default. Sources disagree, so those are marked 'unknown'. Also unverified: whether a municipality can restrict ORVs on provincial highways inside its boundaries.
provincial.router_guidance: Suggested logic: (1) Never route along a Schedule A segment, which includes all 400-series. (2) Provincial 500-899 secondary highways still under MTO: shoulder allowed. (3) Former provincial highways now downloaded to counties or municipalities (e.g. 503, 507, 504, 620, 648, 121) follow the owning municipality's by-law, so check OSM operator/ref tags. (4) Other King's highways: treat as unknown/avoid unless verified. (5) Apply each municipality's rule to its own roads, and the county by-law to county roads.

provincial.crossing_rule: An ORV may be driven directly across a highway (Off-Road Vehicles Act cl. 2(2)(a), recognised in O. Reg. 316/03 s.2): the shortest route, at roughly a right angle, not travelling along it. On-road crossing conditions per OPP/MTO guidance: driver 16+ with G2/M2 or higher, vehicle registered with a rear plate and insured, helmet worn. Caveat: Schedule 1 of R.R.O. 1990 Reg. 863 (ORV Act) was replaced on Jan 1, 2021 by a reference to Schedule A of O. Reg. 316/03 (City of Hamilton memo, Dec 31, 2020). That suggests crossing may also be prohibited on Schedule A highways (e.g. Hwy 28 Apsley-Faraday, Hwy 62 Madoc-Bancroft, Hwy 118 Bracebridge-Haliburton) except perhaps at grade-separated or underpass crossings. Unverified: confirm before routing a crossing of a Schedule A segment. A by-law can also bar crossings of municipal roads or restrict them to set points.
provincial.o_reg_8_03_note: O. Reg. 8/03 lists local municipalities that were townships on Jan 1, 2003. Confirmed in its table from search snippets: Faraday, Hastings Highlands, Tudor and Cashel, Wollaston, Addington Highlands, Admaston/Bromley, Algonquin Highlands, Bonnechere Valley. Most other rural townships in the bbox are probably listed, but this is not verified. Towns and cities (Bancroft, Kawartha Lakes) are not. In listed municipalities with no by-law, compliant ORVs are allowed on municipal roads by default since Jan 1, 2021.

free_riding_notes: Municipal roads that a by-law opens (or 8/03 default-open) need no trail pass. The ORV still needs its plate, insurance, licence and helmet. Confirmed or likely all-road townships: Bancroft, Tudor and Cashel, Highlands East, Algonquin Highlands, Lake of Bays (except listed roads), Havelock-Belmont-Methuen (not Dec 1-Mar 31), North Kawartha (township roads).

Crown land: ORV use is generally allowed on Crown land and existing Crown roads and trails unless restricted by land-use planning, posted signs, or an MNRF road restriction or closure under the Public Lands Act. Building new trails or water crossings, or holding organised events, needs MNRF approval. Not allowed in provincial parks and some conservation reserves.

Provincial parks in or near the bbox (Algonquin, Silent Lake, Bon Echo, Kawartha Highlands Signature Site, Queen Elizabeth II Wildlands, Petroglyphs, etc.) do not permit ORVs except on roads or trails the park designates. Algonquin's Hwy 60 corridor is also Schedule A.
Unopened road allowances are not free riding: Faraday (By-law 21-2024), Tudor and Cashel (2023-34) and South Algonquin (2022-699) require written council approval; HBM prohibits ORVs on them.

Former rail trails owned by townships or counties (Wollaston Rail Trail, Haliburton County Rail Trail, Renfrew County Algonquin/K&P trails, Hastings Heritage Trail) all require a club or alliance pass. Do not route them as free.
North Frontenac historically sold its own permits for township roads and trails into Crown land and wilderness campsites (2008-09). Check current practice.

Forest access roads on Crown land (common north of Bancroft, in Hastings Highlands, South Algonquin, North Frontenac and Addington Highlands) are usually usable for free unless gated or posted. MNRF can restrict specific roads. Licensed forestry roads can be closed during operations.

For any 'unknown' municipality listed in O. Reg. 8/03, the 2021 default suggests its roads are open unless a by-law prohibits. Fewer than ten were actually confirmed in the 8/03 table, so keep these as low confidence.
